explanation: An inference joins details the writer supplies; it does not fill every silence with a guess. In the story, track what Mina says, what she hides, and what she finally does. Her conduct can support a claim about embarrassment even though the narrator never names that feeling.

Two central ideas can develop together without being identical. The equipment note explains both reliable measurement and shared responsibility. Sort details under those two ideas before summarizing; a true detail about a compass is not automatically a complete central idea.

Use a claim, several relevant details, and an explanation of their connection. Do not call a character permanently dishonest because of one concealed mistake. Likewise, an equipment record documents a check, not a guarantee that no later error will occur.

examples.prompt: What suggests that Mina fears being judged?
examples.answer: She hides the map and avoids leading before acknowledging the error.
steps: Locate the relevant evidence: She folds the page in [1] and volunteers for snacks in [2].
Connect that evidence to the question: Both actions reduce opportunities for others to inspect her work.
Check the ending: Mina now shares a qualified correction, so the earlier concealment is a stage in her behavior rather than a permanent character verdict.

examples.prompt: Explain why keeping old maps supports responsible use.
examples.answer: Earlier maps preserve the reason for a correction.
steps: Locate the relevant evidence: Paragraph [3] retains corrected maps and asks for the check that prompted revision.
Connect that evidence to the question: Readers can reconstruct the decision instead of trusting a change blindly.
Check the limitation: retained maps make revision traceable, but the note never promises that the newest version is error-free.

passages.title: The borrowed compass — literature
passages.text:
[1] Mina borrowed the club's compass to mark a trail behind the school. She turned the dial until the red needle pointed toward the painted N, then drew a neat arrow on her map. When the trail bent, her arrow seemed to turn with it. She folded the page before Tomas could see.
[2] At the next meeting she offered to carry the snacks instead of leading. Tomas laid two maps on the table. His creek ran west; hers ran north. "Maybe the creek moved," she said. Nobody laughed. The club adviser asked them to check both maps outside, away from the metal cabinet.
[3] Mina discovered she had confused the dial with the needle. She crossed out her arrow, leaving the first line visible, and wrote how she had corrected it. When a younger student asked which map to trust, Mina handed over hers. "This part has been checked," she said, touching the crossed lines. "The rest still needs us."

passages.title: The borrowed compass — information
passages.text:
Invented school equipment note. [1] A compass needle indicates a direction; rotating the labeled dial does not turn the landscape. Nearby metal may affect a reading. In this club's routine, partners compare readings in an open location, record where they stood, and check a known landmark before drawing a route.
[2] Equipment care also depends on traceable records. The borrower signs the compass out and notes a cracked case or a sticking needle. A later borrower can then separate a damaged tool from an unfamiliar technique. An empty damage box means no problem was reported, not that inspection certainly occurred.
[3] The club keeps corrected maps beside the latest version. This costs storage space but allows another group to understand why a route changed. A correction is useful when it names both the original difficulty and the check that led to revision. Records do not eliminate uncertainty; they make uncertainty easier to investigate.

items.prompt: How does Mina’s joke function in the disagreement?
items.answer: It briefly avoids admitting that a map may be wrong.
steps: The conflicting directions precede "Maybe the creek moved."
A moving creek is offered jokingly rather than supported by evidence.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Choose two details supporting a theme about honest revision.
items.answer: Mina leaves the old line visible and labels what remains unchecked.
steps: She crosses out rather than erases; she says the rest still needs checking.
Both make the limits of her knowledge available to others.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Does Tomas prove his map is correct simply by presenting it?
items.answer: No; the adviser asks them to check both maps.
steps: Two conflicting maps appear before an outdoor check.
Disagreement reveals a problem without establishing the winner.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Write a two-sentence objective summary of Mina’s change.
items.answer: Mina conceals a mistaken compass reading and avoids leading. After checking her method, she shares a corrected map with its limits marked.
steps: Include concealment, investigation, and the final sharing.
Omit judgments such as "Mina is foolish" because they are not plot events.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Why is the younger student’s question important to the ending?
items.answer: It gives Mina a chance to replace concealment with qualified openness.
steps: The student asks which map to trust.
Mina responds by identifying a checked part rather than claiming perfection.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Challenge the claim that Mina becomes certain of every route.
items.answer: Her final statement explicitly leaves part of the map unverified.
steps: She says, "The rest still needs us."
That limitation contradicts total certainty.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Name two distinct central ideas of the equipment note.
items.answer: Readings need checks; shared tools need traceable records.
steps: Paragraph [1] describes comparison; [2]–[3] describe records.
Each idea covers several details rather than one isolated example.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Why does an empty damage box not establish a perfect compass?
items.answer: It may reflect a missing report or inspection.
steps: Paragraph [2] distinguishes no reported problem from certain inspection.
Absence of a record is weaker than a documented check.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Which supports measurement reliability: signing out equipment or checking a landmark? Explain.
items.answer: Checking a landmark directly tests the reading.
steps: The landmark check appears in the measurement routine.
Signing out identifies responsibility but does not test direction.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Paraphrase the final sentence without making records sound useless.
items.answer: Records help people investigate uncertainty even though they cannot remove it entirely.
steps: The note pairs a limitation with a benefit.
Preserve both halves to avoid reversing its meaning.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: What cost accompanies keeping revised maps?
items.answer: Additional storage space.
steps: Paragraph [3] states the storage cost.
The note acknowledges a tradeoff while explaining the records’ value.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Is the note reporting a real research study?
items.answer: No; it is an invented school equipment note.
steps: The opening labels the scenario invented.
Treat its routine as supplied instructional information, not external research evidence.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Explain one way Mina follows the recordkeeping principle.
items.answer: Her visible correction and explanation preserve the change.
steps: The story leaves crossed lines; the note asks for original difficulty and check.
Both make revision understandable to another reader.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: What remains uncertain about the metal cabinet’s role?
items.answer: It may have affected readings, but the story establishes a technique error.
steps: The adviser moves outside; Mina later discovers dial confusion.
A precaution does not prove that the cabinet caused this mistake.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Select a better theme: "Never borrow tools" or "Responsible confidence includes admitting limits." Defend it.
items.answer: The second fits Mina’s checked map and stated uncertainty.
steps: Borrowing continues; Mina shares her work at the end.
The ending values correction rather than avoiding tools.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Write a one-sentence summary that includes both central ideas.
items.answer: The note recommends checking compass readings and documenting tool use and map revisions so others can investigate problems.
steps: Combine the routine in [1] with records in [2]–[3].
Leave out minor examples while retaining their purposes.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Propose a text-grounded question the club could investigate next.
items.answer: Sample: Which remaining map sections can partners verify against landmarks?
steps: Mina leaves parts unchecked; the note supplies landmark checks.
The question is answerable through the stated routine, unlike guessing motives.

items.skill: Build an inference from several separated details
items.prompt: Distinguish one fact of the story from one supported interpretation.
items.answer: Fact: Mina volunteers to carry snacks. Interpretation: she wants to avoid exposing her mistake.
steps: The action is stated in [2]; her motive is not directly named.
The hidden map and timing support, but do not literally state, the motive.

explanation: A theme is a claim about experience, not a topic word such as friendship. Watch the chair’s changing role: reserved space first excludes newcomers, then becomes an invitation. Repeated objects help readers see an idea develop across a story.

An objective summary selects the beginning problem, consequential change, and outcome. It does not retell every movement or praise a favorite character. For information, combine related details into central ideas while keeping limits such as the small sample and uneven attendance.

A pattern can change without every problem disappearing. The narrator still misses Jae at the ending. Explain how grief and welcome can coexist; do not force the story into a lesson that welcoming someone requires forgetting someone else.

examples.prompt: Explain how the loose stone develops the narrator’s understanding.
examples.answer: It reveals that familiar routines can hide another person’s needs.
steps: Locate the relevant evidence: The narrator automatically avoids the stone; Noor marks it for others.
Connect that evidence to the question: Her action shifts attention from private habit to shared access.
Test the alternative that the stone merely delays the walk: Noor marks it for other people, making consideration for unfamiliar users central.

examples.prompt: Why are the two survey results insufficient to show universal inclusion?
examples.answer: Only seven of the original twelve respond later, and guide use is not the same as belonging.
steps: Locate the relevant evidence: Five responses are missing; six report using a guide.
Connect that evidence to the question: Both response coverage and the measured outcome limit the conclusion.
Check the measured outcome: reported guide use does not directly measure whether respondents feel included.

passages.title: The empty chair — literature
passages.text:
[1] Every lunch, I put my jacket on the chair beside me. Jae had moved away three weeks earlier, but our table still looked right with two places occupied. When Noor asked whether anyone was sitting there, I said, "Sort of." She carried her tray to the window.
[2] Our adviser asked me to show Noor the greenhouse. I knew the route Jae and I had used, including the loose paving stone we always avoided. Noor stopped at the stone and chalked a small arrow beside it. "Someone else might trip," she said. I had stepped around it so often that I no longer imagined someone who did not know.
[3] The next day I hung my jacket on the back of my own chair. Noor sat down, and I told her about the time Jae had filled a watering can with a spider inside it. She laughed, then told me a story of her own. At the window, I could still see the empty place where she had eaten yesterday. I missed Jae. For the first time that week, missing him did not take up every seat.

passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original instructional text; invented scenarios and data are labeled in the text.
passages.title: The empty chair — information
passages.text:
Invented club reflection. [1] A welcome survey asked twelve new members which routines had been explained. Nine knew where supplies were stored; four knew how to borrow them. The club therefore separated finding equipment from receiving permission to use it. A tour alone did not communicate both.
[2] Returning members proposed a buddy system, but two newcomers warned that a permanent buddy could prevent them from meeting other people. The revised plan pairs students for their first two meetings and then lets them request more help. A posted borrowing guide gives everyone access to the same instructions.
[3] After one month, seven newcomers answered a follow-up survey. Six reported using the guide. That response suggests the guide reached some members, but five original respondents did not answer again. The club cannot conclude that every newcomer felt included. It plans to ask about both access to information and freedom to participate.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: What does "Sort of" reveal about the first chair?
items.answer: The narrator treats an absent friend’s place as still occupied.
steps: Jae has moved away, but the jacket blocks the seat.
The hesitant answer joins emotional attachment to physical exclusion.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Identify the turning action between isolation and welcome.
items.answer: Moving the jacket to the narrator’s own chair opens the neighboring place.
steps: The action begins [3].
The gesture changes what Noor can do without requiring a speech.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: How does the spider story complicate a theme of moving on?
items.answer: Remembering Jae becomes part of welcoming Noor.
steps: The narrator tells Jae’s story while Noor joins the table.
New friendship and remembrance are compatible.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Explain the final metaphor about missing Jae taking every seat.
items.answer: Grief had crowded out opportunities for companionship.
steps: The narrator still misses Jae but now shares lunch.
Emotional space is represented by the physical seating arrangement.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Which earlier detail prepares the final window image?
items.answer: Noor initially eats by the window.
steps: Paragraph [1] places her there; [3] recalls that place.
The repeated location makes the change in belonging visible.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Summarize the narrator’s development without declaring the grief cured.
items.answer: The narrator initially protects an absent friend’s place, learns from Noor’s consideration, and makes room for her while still missing Jae.
steps: Use the jacket, stone, and final admission.
The summary preserves change and its limit.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: What distinction do the first survey numbers reveal?
items.answer: Knowing supply locations differs from knowing borrowing rules.
steps: Nine know locations; only four know borrowing procedures.
Different questions measure different forms of access.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Trace how criticism changes the buddy proposal.
items.answer: A permanent pairing becomes an initial two-meeting pairing with optional support.
steps: Two newcomers raise concern about meeting others.
The revision responds to dependence while retaining assistance.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Name two central ideas, each supported by a different section.
items.answer: Clear instructions support access; welcoming systems should preserve independence.
steps: The borrowing guide supplies information; optional help replaces permanent buddies.
The ideas are related but address different needs.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Why is the posted guide more than a substitute for a friendly person?
items.answer: It makes the same instructions available to everyone.
steps: Paragraph [2] explicitly describes common access.
Members need not depend entirely on one partner’s knowledge.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Correct "Six of twelve used the guide."
items.answer: Six of seven follow-up respondents reported using it; use by the others is unknown.
steps: The follow-up has seven respondents, not twelve.
Separate respondents from the original group and reports from direct observation.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: What should an objective summary omit: survey limits or "the wonderful plan"?
items.answer: Omit the praise, retain the survey limits.
steps: The text reports nonresponses but does not call the plan wonderful.
Limits affect what the information means; praise adds evaluation.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Compare Noor’s arrow with the club’s guide.
items.answer: Both make formerly insider knowledge visible to others.
steps: Noor marks the hazard; the club posts borrowing instructions.
Each reduces dependence on someone already knowing the routine.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Where do the texts resist an all-or-nothing conclusion?
items.answer: The narrator still misses Jae; the club cannot say everyone feels included.
steps: Both endings retain an unresolved condition.
Improvement does not establish complete resolution.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Draft a useful follow-up survey question about freedom.
items.answer: Sample: After two meetings, could you choose activities and partners without unwanted assistance?
steps: The revised plan limits obligatory pairing.
The question measures freedom rather than merely guide use.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Would deleting the first window scene weaken the ending? Explain.
items.answer: Yes; the final empty window place would lose its contrast with Noor’s earlier isolation.
steps: The same location is shown before and after her move.
Structural recurrence helps develop the theme.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Give an evidence-based claim about welcome with a qualification.
items.answer: Welcome can involve changing routines, though a single change does not prove everyone feels included.
steps: The jacket and buddy plan change; the follow-up remains incomplete.
A qualified claim respects both kinds of evidence.

items.skill: Trace a theme through a changing pattern
items.prompt: Offer another defensible theme besides making room for others.
items.answer: Sample: Another person’s perspective can expose unnoticed habits.
steps: Noor marks a stone the narrator automatically avoids.
An alternative must explain a meaningful pattern rather than name a topic.

explanation: Information may develop two central ideas by alternating examples. Here the school’s roof trial concerns both measurement and decision-making. Label what each sentence contributes before joining the ideas; the rain barrel is a setting, not the whole explanation.

Literary details can develop a parallel question without functioning as scientific evidence. A leaking cardboard city helps Leon rethink a perfect-looking model, but this imagined event cannot prove a real roof design works. Use the story for theme and the technical note for its stated trial.

An exact number can be accurately read and still be overinterpreted. Check units, conditions, and the population observed. The supplied data compare one trial under stated conditions; words such as always and guarantees demand broader support than this record supplies.

examples.prompt: Why does the photograph matter more than a flawless display?
examples.answer: It lets Leon discuss a failure and invite investigation.
steps: Locate the relevant evidence: Visitors study the wet model; Leon explains the seam and asks about future leaks.
Connect that evidence to the question: The display becomes a source of questions rather than only admiration.
Compare the earlier towel with the later photograph: the same failure is first hidden and then made available for discussion.

examples.prompt: What two central ideas organize the roof note?
examples.answer: Interpret trials within their limits, and judge designs using explicit priorities.
steps: Locate the relevant evidence: Paragraphs [1]–[2] discuss measurement limits; [3] discusses criteria.
Connect that evidence to the question: The ideas connect evidence with decisions without confusing them.
Test a one-idea summary: describing only the winning collection amount would omit the separate discussion of cost and repair criteria.

passages.title: Rain on the roof — literature
passages.text:
[1] Leon’s cardboard city had mirrored towers and a roof garden made from green felt. He placed it beside Sana’s low, untidy model. "Mine looks like a city people would choose," he said. Sana pressed a finger into a paper channel running down her roof. "Mine tells the water where to go."
[2] For the demonstration, their teacher poured the same small cup of water over each model. Leon’s felt darkened. A hidden seam opened, and a paper apartment sagged. He reached for a towel, hoping to cover the collapsed wall. Sana’s channel carried water into a bottle cap, although some escaped over its edge.
[3] At the exhibition Leon placed a photograph of the wet model beside his repaired city. Visitors looked longer at the photograph than at the towers. He explained the seam and asked where they thought the next leak might occur. Sana lent him an extra cap. Neither model stayed completely dry, but both now had somewhere for a question to land.

passages.title: Rain on the roof — information
passages.text:
Invented classroom roof-model record; these models do not establish building safety. [1] Two trays each received 100 mL of water from the same height. Tray A had a flat felt surface. Tray B had a paper channel leading to a collection cup. The class recorded 10 mL in A's cup and 65 mL in B's cup after two minutes. Uncollected water might remain on a tray, spill, or soak into material.
[2] The trial compares collected water under one set of conditions. It does not isolate channel shape from surface material because both changed. Repeating it could show consistency; changing one design feature at a time could make the cause clearer.
[3] Design decisions also require priorities. A model that collects more water might take longer to build or use more material. Before choosing, the class should define whether it values collection, low cost, or ease of repair. A useful record therefore includes both measured results and the criteria used to judge them.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Contrast Leon’s and Sana’s opening priorities.
items.answer: Leon values appearance; Sana emphasizes water movement.
steps: He praises mirrored towers; she points to a channel.
Their dialogue sets up competing design criteria.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: What does reaching for the towel suggest?
items.answer: Leon initially wants to hide the visible failure.
steps: He hopes to cover the collapsed wall.
The stated intention supports embarrassment, not a technical repair yet.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Find evidence that Sana’s design is also imperfect.
items.answer: Some water escapes over the cap’s edge.
steps: Paragraph [2] names the overflow.
The comparison does not make one model universally successful.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Explain the shift from Leon’s statement to his final question.
items.answer: He moves from confident judgment to inviting others’ scrutiny.
steps: The opening says people would choose his city; the ending asks about another leak.
The changed speech supports intellectual openness.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Interpret "somewhere for a question to land."
items.answer: The models now encourage inquiry about how they work.
steps: Leon displays failure and asks visitors for predictions.
The figurative landing place is an opportunity for investigation.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Write a theme supported by both concealment and display.
items.answer: Learning can improve when people expose errors instead of hiding them.
steps: The towel conceals; the photograph makes the flaw public.
The reversal develops the claim across the plot.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: What was held constant in the two-tray comparison?
items.answer: Water amount, pouring height, and observation time.
steps: Both receive 100 mL from the same height and are read after two minutes.
Shared conditions make comparisons more meaningful.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Does 65 mL collected mean all remaining water leaked?
items.answer: No; water could remain, spill, or soak into material.
steps: Paragraph [1] lists three possibilities.
The collection measure does not distinguish them.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: How much more water reached B’s cup, and what does that comparison mean?
items.answer: 55 mL more in this trial.
steps: Subtract 10 mL from 65 mL.
The difference concerns collected water, not overall building safety.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Why can the trial not isolate the channel’s effect?
items.answer: Both channel shape and surface material changed.
steps: Paragraph [2] identifies two changed features.
Either or both could contribute to the result.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Distinguish a result from a criterion in the record.
items.answer: 65 mL is a result; low cost is a possible criterion.
steps: The result was measured; cost is named as a priority for judging designs.
Evidence describes what happened, while criteria define what counts as desirable.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Suggest a fairer follow-up for testing channel shape.
items.answer: Keep material, water, height, and timing constant while varying only channel shape.
steps: The original changes material and shape together.
Controlling material removes that competing explanation.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Can Leon’s experience establish that every failed design improves learning?
items.answer: No; it supports a literary theme, not a universal experimental result.
steps: The story is invented and depicts one productive response.
A broader empirical claim would require different evidence.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Connect the photograph to the note’s recording advice.
items.answer: Both preserve evidence needed to discuss a design choice.
steps: The photograph shows the failure; the note requires results and criteria.
Transparent records let others assess reasoning.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Repair the claim "B is the best design."
items.answer: B collected more water in this trial; other criteria and repeated tests remain unexamined.
steps: Collection differs, but cost and repair are not measured.
Qualifying the claim matches its scope to available evidence.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Which detail best counters "Leon only cares about praise"?
items.answer: He asks visitors to identify the next possible leak.
steps: The final question invites criticism.
An unchanged desire for admiration alone would not explain that invitation well.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Summarize the technical note in two sentences without choosing a winner.
items.answer: A two-tray trial measured different water collection but changed more than one feature. The class needs clearer tests and explicit priorities before making a design judgment.
steps: Include findings, limitations, and criteria.
An objective summary reports the decision problem rather than resolving it without evidence.

items.skill: Separate related central ideas and supporting examples
items.prompt: Name one unanswered question each text leaves.

passages.title: The second inscription — literature
passages.text:
[1] The garden sign read BUILT BY ROOM SEVEN. Eli liked its wide blue letters. His class had moved the benches, dug the beds, and planted the beans. When the caretaker stopped beside the sign, Eli offered him a paintbrush. "You could add a border."
[2] The caretaker looked at the smooth boards. "Those were the old stage steps," he said. "The drama group spent Saturday taking them apart." Eli remembered the stack outside the hall. He had assumed it was scrap nobody wanted. There had been a note under the top board, now probably under the beans.
[3] At the next meeting, Eli suggested repainting the whole sign. A classmate said the beans would not grow faster with more names. "No," Eli answered, "but the next person might know whom to ask before taking the wood." They kept the original line, adding MATERIALS PREPARED BY THE DRAMA GROUP underneath. Eli’s new letters were smaller, but he stood farther back to make sure they could still be read.

passages.title: The second inscription — information
passages.text:
Original source-reading guide. [1] A retrospective autobiography tells events from the perspective of a person looking back on their own life. It can provide direct access to that writer's remembered actions and judgments. It is not a transcript of every conversation, and its author chooses which episodes to include.
[2] In source h, Franklin describes a practical project and a moral correction. A careful reader can report that he says the boys moved stones and his father objected. The reader should not invent the workmen's private thoughts or assume the source records every participant's account.
[3] Separate the sequence from the interpretation: muddy ground motivates a project; the boys take material; the loss is traced; a parent challenges the defense of usefulness. The sequence supports an explanation of how the problem developed. Franklin's final remembered lesson supplies his interpretation of why the episode mattered.

passages.title: Franklin recalls a childhood wharf
passages.text: There was a salt-marsh that bounded part of the mill-pond, on the edge of which, at high water, we used to stand to fish for minnows. By much trampling, we had made it a mere quagmire. My proposal was to build a wharf there fit for us to stand upon, and I showed my comrades a large heap of stones, which were intended for a new house near the marsh, and which would very well suit our purpose. Accordingly, in the evening, when the workmen were gone, I assembled a number of my playfellows, and working with them diligently like so many emmets, sometimes two or three to a stone, we brought them all away and built our little wharf. The next morning the workmen were surprised at missing the stones, which were found in our wharf. Inquiry was made after the removers; we were discovered and complained of; several of us were corrected by our fathers; and, though I pleaded the usefulness of the work, mine convinced me that nothing was useful which was not honest.

passages.title: The quiet rehearsal — literature
passages.text:
[1] Imani could play the drum roll faster than anyone in the ensemble. During the first rehearsal she filled every gap with a flourish. Across the room, the violinists stopped twice. "We can’t hear the entrance," one said. Imani looked at the conductor, waiting to be defended.
[2] Instead, the conductor asked everyone to play four measures without Imani. The melody seemed thin to her, but she heard a soft breath before the violins began. When she returned, she left that space empty. Her hands hovered above the drumhead, suddenly awkward without something to prove.
[3] At the performance, a chair scraped loudly just before the entrance. Imani’s fingers twitched toward a roll that could cover the noise. She held them still. The conductor lifted a hand; the violins entered together. Afterward a friend said, "I hardly noticed your best part." Imani looked at the quiet drum and smiled. "That may have been the best part."

passages.title: The quiet rehearsal — information
passages.text:
Invented ensemble observation note. [1] A cue is a signal that tells performers when to act. In a classroom rehearsal, a visible raised hand can provide a shared starting point even when a quiet breath is hard to hear. A cue works only if performers know its meaning and can perceive it.
[2] The observer recorded three entrances: first, two players began early; second, everyone began after the raised hand; third, one player watched the score and entered late. These are observations, not proof that the hand signal caused every result. The record does not measure each player's view or attention.
[3] A useful rehearsal report separates what happened from a proposed explanation. "One player entered late" records an event. "The player could not see the hand" is a hypothesis unless checked. The group can ask where players were looking or repeat the entrance with a clearer sightline. Rehearsal notes support improvement when they preserve this distinction instead of assigning blame too quickly.

passages.title: The unfinished mural — literature
passages.text:
[1] Amara painted a river along the community-room wall, leaving a rectangle for the old footbridge. Her grandfather wanted the bridge shown as he remembered it: a meeting place with flower boxes. Her neighbor Kit remembered the loose rail that had kept her from crossing with a stroller. "Paint both," Amara said, then discovered that a flower box could hide the rail.
[2] She tried a version with no people and no broken wood. It was beautiful and strangely empty. At the open studio, Grandfather described a picnic; Kit described carrying groceries around the longer road. Other visitors added memories that would not fit inside one rectangle. Amara taped their words beside her sketch.
[3] On the final evening, she painted the bridge’s outline but left part of the rail unfinished. A label invited visitors to read the accounts and suggest details for a later panel. "You haven’t decided what it was," Grandfather said. Amara rinsed her brush. "I’ve decided it wasn’t the same place for everyone." The unfinished patch no longer looked to her like an absence. It looked like space she had stopped taking for herself.

passages.title: The unfinished mural — information
passages.text:
Invented community art proposal. [1] A committee can document a decision without claiming agreement that never occurred. Its record should separate the proposal, reasons offered, objections, and the action chosen. Names may be replaced with roles when personal identification is unnecessary.
[2] In this scenario, twelve participants discuss a mural. Seven favor completing one shared image now, three favor separate panels, and two want more time. These are preferences among the participants present, not a survey of every resident. The committee chooses an initial outline and a later comment period; the numbers alone do not explain why that compromise was selected.
[3] Public comments may reveal experiences absent from the first meeting, but a comment box does not guarantee that everyone can participate. Written instructions, an oral response option, and a stated closing date can make the process clearer. The final record should describe which comments influenced revision and which issues remain unsettled.

explanation: Setting is more than scenery when it changes what a character can do. List the ferry’s departure, the island’s limited route, and the rising wind before explaining Mara’s decision. A causal account links a condition to an available choice and then to a consequence.

Informational sections also interact. The route notice first establishes service, then gives an exception, then explains how updates reach travelers. Read the exception before applying the ordinary schedule; a general rule does not cancel a specific condition.

A character may act from several motives. Mara’s return serves both the forgotten instrument and a promise. Name the evidence for each without claiming the storm alone determines her behavior. Conditions constrain action; they do not erase agency.

passages.title: The last ferry — literature
passages.text:
[1] The island ferry sounded its first horn while Mara stood outside the music room. The path to the landing took six minutes; boarding closed in eight. She had promised to bring the school’s violin to the mainland concert. Through the window she could see its case beneath a chair. Her bag held the key.
[2] A gust folded the notice on the door against the glass. Across the square, her cousin waved from the path. "There’s another boat tomorrow!" he called. Mara thought of the empty chair the orchestra would leave for her and of the younger player who had lent her a bow. She unlocked the room.
[3] When she reached the landing, the gate was shut. The ferry had left early under a wind warning. Her cousin was still there; he had waited. Mara sat on the case until the harbor worker asked her to move it away from the wet edge. She stood up, then opened it. If she could not reach the concert, she could at least play the difficult passage for the person who had stayed.

passages.title: The last ferry — information
passages.text:
Invented island transport notice. [1] Ordinary service: the afternoon ferry departs at 4:00; boarding normally closes two minutes earlier. Walking from the school to the landing takes about six minutes. This estimate assumes no stops and ordinary walking conditions.
[2] Weather exception: the harbor supervisor may close boarding or move departure earlier when wind threatens safe operation. The posted schedule is therefore not a guarantee. A warning displayed at the landing applies even if an older notice elsewhere remains visible.
[3] Update procedure: staff post a warning at the landing and notify the school office. Travelers should confirm current service before leaving the school. A missed ferry does not entitle someone to open a closed gate. The notice explains travel arrangements; it does not describe every traveler’s reasons for making the journey.

explanation: In drama, stage directions supply actions and spatial information that a narrator might otherwise explain. Track who can hear each line and which door is open. A pause or movement can alter meaning even when dialogue stays unchanged.

An informational explanation can organize a process by functions rather than chronology. The theater note separates sightlines, entrances, and accessibility. Ask what each section adds to the shared problem of helping an audience follow action.

A stage choice is an interpretation supported by words and directions. Do not invent facial expressions as though they were printed facts. When proposing a performance, label additions as choices and explain how they could emphasize a supported conflict.

passages.title: One room, two doors — literature
passages.text:
Original short play, complete scene.
[1] A community-room stage has a street door on the left and a kitchen door on the right. A table stands between them. Jo holds a sealed envelope. Ren stacks cups by the kitchen.
JO: If I put it here, she will find it.
REN: If you put it there, you can leave before she does.
[Jo sets the envelope down, then places a cup on top of it.]
[2] JO: I said I would explain why I left the team.
REN: Paper cannot answer her questions.
[A knock at the street door. Jo takes one step toward the kitchen. Ren moves the cups from the envelope but does not block either door.]
JO: You could tell her I already went.
REN: I could.
[A second knock.]
[3] Jo returns to the table, picks up the envelope, and opens the street door.
JO: I wrote this so I wouldn’t forget. But I can stay while you read.
[Ren carries the cups into the kitchen. The street door remains open.]

passages.title: One room, two doors — information
passages.text:
Original theater design note. [1] Sightlines are the paths along which an audience can see stage action. A high object at the center can hide a hand movement from some seats. Designers therefore test important actions from several positions, not only from the center aisle.
[2] Entrances create expectations. Two visible doors can make a choice legible: a character can approach one and reverse toward the other. If one door is hidden, that same movement may seem accidental. The physical plan helps communicate the action’s structure.
[3] Access affects both performers and audiences. Clear routes help performers move without relying on an unseen obstacle. Spoken information or an audio description can communicate a silent action to someone who cannot see it. A design explanation should identify which information is visual and what another mode must convey, rather than assuming everyone receives the same cues.

passages.title: Fourteen lines at dusk — literature
passages.text:
Original fourteen-line poem; grouped as three quatrains and a couplet, without strict meter.
1 I brought a jar to gather all the light,
2 a lid to keep the afternoon inside;
3 I held it where the windows burned most bright
4 and watched the golden color slip aside.

5 I wrote the names of birds I thought I knew,
6 then heard a call no name could quite contain.
7 The page was full; the sky kept coming through,
8 a wider blue beyond my tidy chain.

9 So now I leave a margin on the page,
10 a little field no answer has to own.
11 The evening does not fit inside a cage;
12 the seed is not the same thing as the grown.

13 I close the book, but leave one question wide:
14 what waits beyond the names I put inside?

passages.attribution: Written for Liminal. Original instructional text; invented scenarios and data are labeled in the text.
passages.title: Fourteen lines at dusk — information
passages.text:
Original field-notebook guide. [1] A list of names can organize observations, but a mistaken label may hide a difference worth investigating. A reader should distinguish a confident identification from a tentative one. Writing "unidentified call" preserves an observation without pretending to know its source.
[2] Divide a notebook entry into observation, possible identification, and next question. For example: "three short calls from a hidden branch"; "possibly the bird seen nearby"; "can I observe the caller next time?" These are invented sample notes, not a report of a particular species.
[3] A notebook cannot preserve every feature of an outdoor event. Sound, motion, and distance may be difficult to describe. Sketches and time notes can help, but the writer should state uncertainty. The routine aims to make later inquiry possible, not to turn incomplete observations into complete knowledge.

passages.title: The paper bridge — literature
passages.text:
[1] Niko’s paper bridge held sixteen counters before bending. At the next table, Tessa’s held seven. Niko wrote 16 in a large square and began drawing a medal around it. Beneath his bridge, a folded scrap rested on the table, touching the span at its center.
[2] Tessa crouched to see how he had folded the paper. "Is that part of the design?" she asked. Niko pushed the scrap into his pocket. "It was just there." The teacher did not erase his number. She drew a small asterisk and asked him to describe every support.
[3] In the second test, Niko removed the scrap before placing any counters. His bridge held six. He wrote both results, labeling one "center support" and the other "open span." Tessa drew two little diagrams beside them. The large square on Niko’s sheet still held 16, but the medal had become a frame around an explanation.

passages.title: The paper bridge — information
passages.text:
Invented paper-bridge procedure and record. [1] Place two equal-height books 12 cm apart on a table. Lay one sheet of paper across the gap. Keep its folds unchanged during one trial. Do not place a support under the gap. These conditions define the open-span test.
[2] Add identical counters one at a time at the center. Stop when the paper touches the table; record only the number held before that touch. Remove all counters before changing the folds. Repeat under the same conditions to check consistency.
[3] Example record: trial A held 6 counters before contact; the seventh caused contact. Trial B held 8 before contact; the ninth caused contact. These invented results do not establish a best fold. A report should label changes in fold, span, or support, because different conditions answer different questions.

explanation: A historical account often combines a sequence with the writer’s explanation of it. Franklin’s account moves from a club’s shared books to their separation. Track the original reason, the benefit, and the care problem; later events do not erase earlier usefulness.

The fictional shelf story also turns on a missing system. The locked cupboard changes access, but the ending supplies a procedure instead of treating every lock as the enemy. Explain how setting and rules interact to shape choices.

A source’s order can make a problem intelligible. Read the original excerpt before the modern guide, then check whether the guide preserves its qualification: books were useful even though the collection was eventually divided. Avoid replacing a mixed outcome with a simple success or failure label.

passages.title: A shelf and a system — literature
passages.text:
[1] Every lunch, Lian unlocked the club cupboard with a key tied to her wrist. Inside stood twelve shared sketchbooks. She liked knowing exactly where each one belonged. When she missed a week of school, nobody drew in them.
[2] On returning, she found a pile of loose drawings under the cupboard. "We didn’t want to lose anything," Sam said. Lian spread them across the table. Some had no names. Two showed different halves of the same imagined town, but their artists had never seen each other’s pages.
[3] Lian proposed leaving the cupboard open. Sam asked who would remember which book had gone home. They made a sign-out card and put a spare key in the office. On Friday, Lian watched someone else open the door. A sketchbook was on the wrong shelf, and she nearly corrected it before noticing a new bridge connecting the town’s two halves.

passages.title: A shelf and a system — information
passages.text:
Original historical reading guide. [1] In source h, Franklin recalls club members combining books so they could consult them during discussion. The account names shared access as an expected benefit. It also says the collection was smaller than expected.
[2] A sequence map should retain both the use and the difficulty: proposal, agreement, collection, useful consultation, insufficient care, separation after about a year. The source does not specify every care problem. Missing labels, theft, and water damage are possible problems in libraries generally, but none should be inserted as facts about this collection.
[3] A modern reader can ask what system might address care while preserving access. That question uses the historical account as a starting point; an invented modern solution is not evidence of what these members actually tried. Keep historical description and present-day proposal in separate sentences.

passages.attribution: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography (written 1771–1790), 1916 edition edited by Frank Woodworth Pine. Public domain in the United States; original spelling retained, editorial footnote markers removed.
passages.title: Franklin — historical source excerpt
passages.text: About this time, our club meeting, not at a tavern, but in a little room of Mr. Grace's, set apart for that purpose, a proposition was made by me, that, since our books were often referr'd to in our disquisitions upon the queries, it might be convenient to us to have them altogether where we met, that upon occasion they might be consulted; and by thus clubbing our books to a common library, we should, while we lik'd to keep them together, have each of us the advantage of using the books of all the other members, which would be nearly as beneficial as if each owned the whole. It was lik'd and agreed to, and we fill'd one end of the room with such books as we could best spare. The number was not so great as we expected; and tho' they had been of great use, yet some inconveniences occurring for want of due care of them, the collection, after about a year, was separated, and each took his books home again.

explanation: Authors choose where readers receive crucial information. A late explanation can make readers reinterpret an earlier scene. This week compare the order of events with the order of disclosure: the map is drawn before its purpose is understood.

Information can use the same evidence in different orders. A result-first report quickly states a finding; a method-first report foregrounds how the finding was obtained. Neither order by itself proves reliability. Check whether all necessary conditions remain available.

An analysis of structure names a part, explains its contribution, and considers a plausible alternative order. Avoid saying only that a paragraph adds detail. Identify the particular misunderstanding it resolves or the expectation it creates.

passages.title: The map in the middle — literature
passages.text:
[1] For three afternoons, Dev drew the courtyard without including its fountain. His classmates teased him about forgetting the largest object. He measured the side path, marked a bench, and placed a blue dot near the gate. When asked about the fountain, he covered the middle of the page with his hand.
[2] On Thursday his grandmother visited. She stopped at the gate with her walking frame. Dev unfolded the map. Its blue dots marked places to pause; its wide lines showed routes with room to turn. The fountain’s edge narrowed one route so sharply that she could not use it comfortably.
[3] Dev finally drew the fountain, not as the center of a postcard but as a curved boundary beside a path. His classmates helped check the other corners. The map was less beautiful than their first guesses about it. It was also the first courtyard map his grandmother asked to keep.

passages.title: The map in the middle — information
passages.text:
Invented route-study report, in three sections. [1] Result: two of four courtyard routes met the club’s stated turning-space requirement for its cardboard model. This model result is not a guarantee of access for every person or mobility device.
[2] Method: students drew four routes on a scale plan and moved a fixed-width cardboard shape along each. A route counted as passing only if the shape could turn at every marked corner without crossing a boundary. They did not test slopes or surface condition.
[3] Next step: inspect the real routes with the people who will use them, checking conditions the model omitted. A summary for quick planning might lead with the result; a technical record might lead with the method. Either should retain the limited scope and the untested factors.

passages.title: Click, clatter, hush — literature
passages.text:
Original poem.
[1] Click, clatter, click: the late bus climbs.
Its windows rattle little borrowed rhymes.
I count the cracks between the crowded seats;
the engine eats the evening, street by street.

[2] At every stop the folding doorway sighs.
A paper ticket flutters, lifts, and lies.
Then someone hums a tune I almost know;
my counting loses time, the traffic slows.

[3] Hush. Not the bus—the bus is booming still.
A child's small question crosses all that steel:
"Does everyone get home?" The doors draw wide.
I leave a little silence at my side.

passages.title: Click, clatter, hush — information
passages.text:
Original sound-reading note; no sound measurements are reported here. [1] A sound meter can record a physical quantity under specified conditions, but the experience of loudness also depends on the listener and the sound. A reading taken close to a source cannot be compared fairly with a distant reading unless that difference is considered.
[2] In everyday speech, "quiet" may mean low sound level, little conversation, or concentrated attention. In a poem, a speaker may call a moment quiet while machinery continues. Readers should use nearby words to decide which meaning is intended.
[3] A useful comparison therefore identifies both the question and the evidence. To compare meter readings, state distance, timing, and the quantity measured. To interpret a poem’s hush, attend to the speaker’s changed focus. Neither type of evidence automatically answers the other type of question.

passages.title: Two views of the orchard — literature
passages.text:
Original paired monologues.
[1] ADA: My grandfather planted the crooked tree beside the gate. When we were small, its low branch was the only ladder we needed. People now call it an obstruction. I know the path bends around it, but that bend is where visitors pause long enough to see the orchard. If we straighten everything, what will remind us that people were here before the plan?
[2] FINN: I like the tree, too. Last week I helped push a cart around it, and one wheel sank into the wet edge. Ada says the bend makes people pause. It made us unload three boxes. I am not asking for every tree to stand like a soldier. I am asking for a dry way past this one.
[3] ADA: When Finn brought the empty cart to the meeting, I wanted to tell another story about Grandfather. Instead, I helped him turn it. There was room if we moved the fence a little. I still touched the low branch before leaving.

passages.title: Two views of the orchard — information
passages.text:
Invented orchard planning commentary. [1] Some members argue that straight paths would improve cart access; others fear losing the orchard’s familiar character. Both concerns describe real priorities within this scenario, but neither alone determines which physical changes are necessary.
[2] The writer recommends testing a small fence adjustment before removing the crooked tree. Although a straight path might shorten the route, the supplied account identifies a local bottleneck rather than a need to straighten every path. A trial can ask whether carts can pass without entering the wet edge.
[3] If the adjustment works, it may preserve the tree while improving access. If it does not, the committee should consider other routes. This is a conditional proposal, not a promise that one inexpensive change will solve every problem. The evidence needed is a route test, not a vote on whose memories matter more.

passages.title: The narrator’s umbrella — literature
passages.text:
[1] I knew why Ms. Vale always stood at the crossing with that enormous umbrella. She enjoyed making people wait. Every morning she raised her palm just when I had gathered enough speed to coast my bicycle through. "A professional obstacle," I told my brother.
[2] On Tuesday I arrived early. Ms. Vale was kneeling beside the curb, collecting small pieces of glass into a paper bag. A delivery van turned so close that its mirror almost touched her umbrella. She raised the umbrella higher. Behind it, a child in a yellow coat stepped back from the road.
[3] Later, when her palm rose in front of me, I noticed her eyes moving toward a car hidden behind the van. I put one foot down. My brother asked whether the obstacle was working late. "She’s watching something we can’t see," I said. It was not an apology, exactly. But the next morning I brought her a stronger bag.

passages.title: The narrator’s umbrella — information
passages.text:
Original observation guide. [1] An observation reports something perceived: a person raises a hand, a bicycle stops, or glass lies beside a curb. An inference proposes what an observation means. A character label such as "bossy" packages an inference about motives or habits.
[2] To test a label, look for competing explanations. A raised hand might express control, warn about traffic, or signal someone across the street. Nearby events can strengthen one explanation. One isolated movement rarely establishes a permanent trait.
[3] Revision does not require pretending the first observation never occurred. The bicycle really stopped; the explanation for the stop may change. A careful account can say what was seen, what was first assumed, and what later evidence prompted a different judgment.

passages.title: Whose garden after sunset? — literature
passages.text:
[1] "At sunset the garden finally belongs to the birds," said Leo, rolling the hose. He wanted the gate locked early. Across the bed, Mira lifted a basket of beans. "At sunset my mother finally gets home," she said. "If you close it then, she only sees our garden from the street."
[2] Leo pointed to flattened seedlings beside the bench. Last Friday’s gathering had spread beyond the path. Mira did not defend the damage. She picked up a snapped stem and said, "Then make a rule about the beds, not about the hour when she can come."
[3] They sat quietly while the light moved up the wall. Leo had pictured a gate protecting something delicate. Mira had pictured the same gate separating people from work they had helped begin. Before leaving, they moved the bench closer to the path. Neither called that a complete solution, but both stayed long enough to test whether there was room to sit without stepping on the soil.

passages.text:
Invented editorial. [1] Supporters of an early garden closing argue that evening gatherings threaten seedlings and disturb quiet. The damaged plants in this scenario give their concern a concrete basis. The writer agrees that protecting beds matters.
[2] However, a sunset closing would also exclude members whose work ends late. Damage observed during one gathering does not establish that every evening visitor causes damage. The writer favors keeping the garden open for a two-week trial with marked seating and a clear path rule.
[3] Record path use, plant damage, and complaints during the trial. If problems persist, revise the plan. Calling the proposal "unlimited access" would misrepresent it: the proposal has rules, a short duration, and a review. The aim is to test a narrower response before applying a broad restriction.

passages.title: The name on the proposal — literature
passages.text:
[1] Bea wrote her name above the recycling plan in letters larger than the title. She had spent three evenings counting bins. At the meeting, the chair introduced it as "Bea’s project," and everyone began asking Bea what she would do about the crowded hallway, missing lids, and Friday pickup.
[2] She had answers for only two questions. Kofi offered a diagram of another bin location. Bea almost said that the diagram was not part of her plan. Instead she slid her paper beside his and crossed out the possessive word in the title. "Could this be our trial?" she asked.
[3] When the trial succeeded in one corridor, the newsletter named the whole committee. Bea clipped the paragraph and pinned it over her original draft. Sometimes she lifted the clipping to see her large name beneath it. She was pleased with the corridor. She was not yet as indifferent to the credit as she wished.

passages.title: The name on the proposal — information
passages.text:
Original source guide. [1] In source h, Franklin describes seeking commitments for a subscription library. His words "objections and reluctances" identify resistance from potential supporters. He presents his reduced visibility as a response to that resistance.
[2] "Vanity" here means pride in one's own importance or recognition. "Merit" refers to deserving credit. The feather image at the end treats claimed credit like decoration that can be taken from one person and returned to another.
[3] The passage moves from remembered difficulty to personal strategy to advice for readers. Its confident recommendation is itself part of Franklin's self-presentation. The source shows how he explains his experience; it does not provide a controlled comparison proving that every anonymous proposal succeeds.

passages.title: Franklin — historical source excerpt
passages.text: The objections and reluctances I met with in soliciting the subscriptions, made me soon feel the impropriety of presenting one's self as the proposer of any useful project, that might be suppos'd to raise one's reputation in the smallest degree above that of one's neighbours, when one has need of their assistance to accomplish that project. I therefore put myself as much as I could out of sight, and stated it as a scheme of a number of friends, who had requested me to go about and propose it to such as they thought lovers of reading. In this way my affair went on more smoothly, and I ever after practis'd it on such occasions; and, from my frequent successes, can heartily recommend it. The present little sacrifice of your vanity will afterwards be amply repaid. If it remains a while uncertain to whom the merit belongs, someone more vain than yourself will be encouraged to claim it, and then even envy will be disposed to do you justice by plucking those assumed feathers, and restoring them to their right owner.

passages.text:
[1] "The dark cover wins," said Ellis, holding up the temperature chart. Jo kept her finger on the heading: model-box trial. The boxes had stood under the same classroom lamp, but one thermometer had marks farther apart than the other.
[2] Ellis drafted the announcement: DARK ROOFS MAKE EVERY ROOM HOTTER. Jo wrote a smaller sentence beneath it: In our model, the covered boxes differed at the final reading. "Nobody will read that," Ellis said. "They might believe the other one," Jo answered.
[3] They borrowed matching thermometers and repeated the trial. The dark-covered box again ended warmer, though the difference was smaller. Ellis erased every room. passages.text:
Invented technical record. [1] Two model boxes use matching thermometers with 1°C divisions. The word detectable in this record means a difference of at least one marked division, not proof of importance in a real building. Under the same lamp for ten minutes, box D reads 27°C and box P reads 25°C.
[2] A repeat under the same stated conditions gives D = 26°C and P = 25°C. Both trials show D higher; the size of the difference changes. The record does not supply insulation, outdoor weather, or room measurements.
[3] The purpose is to compare these model readings and identify a question for further testing. A reader may say the differences were detectable on this scale. A reader may not conclude that every real room would warm by a fixed amount. Measurement precision, consistency, and practical importance are related but different questions.

passages.text:
[1] Oren kept the workshop key on a red cord. When Asha asked to open the room for Saturday’s repair session, he heard the question as a request for his place in the group. He had always been the person who arrived first.

passages.text:
[1] The workshop bell bit into Nessa’s explanation. Everyone reached for a coat except Hal, who held two loose wires above his cardboard model. "One minute," he said. Nessa had spent the meeting waiting for her turn to explain how the model worked. The bell seemed to take the last sentence from her mouth.
[2] Their mentor stopped at the door. "That bell tells us when to check the room, not when to stop listening." She set down her bag. Hal lowered the wires. Nessa looked at the clock, then at the people still standing.
[3] She finished in three sentences. This time she began with the question the model was meant to answer. When the group finally left, Hal held the door while she carried the model. The bell had not changed its note. It had changed its job.

passages.text:
Invented scheduling argument. [1] A club proposes a bell five minutes before closing to remind members to clean the room. In a one-day trial, fourteen of sixteen present members reported hearing it. Eleven reported beginning cleanup. These are self-reports from one meeting.
[2] A supporter says the bell therefore guarantees a tidy room. That conclusion is stronger than the evidence: hearing a signal is not completing cleanup, and the room’s final condition was not recorded. The trial does support asking whether the reminder helps members begin.
[3] A stronger follow-up would record what tasks were finished and whether instructions were clear, while keeping the closing routine consistent. Members should also have a visible reminder so that the routine does not depend only on hearing a sound.

passages.text:
[1] Zuri stood on a crate and painted the fence a fierce yellow. From the street, she looked like the only person working. Behind the fence, three neighbors sanded boards and mixed paint where passing drivers could not see them.
[2] A visitor asked to take her picture for the neighborhood page. Zuri had imagined that moment all morning. She lifted the brush, then noticed a pale handprint on her sleeve where Mr. Chen had steadied the crate. "Wait," she said. She climbed down and opened the gate.

A wider image from the same moment shows that two labeled bins nearby are sorted correctly and the full bin is temporarily holding unsorted delivery packaging.
[2] The close photograph is relevant to that one bin’s condition, but insufficient for a claim about everyone’s habits. The wider view does not prove sorting is perfect either. It changes the context and reveals that the original caption generalizes beyond the image.
[3] A responsible caption identifies place, time, and what the image actually shows. Further claims about routine sorting need observations across bins and occasions. Cropping is not always deceptive; it becomes misleading when the selected view is asked to support a conclusion it cannot establish.

passages.title: The enormous little bar — literature
passages.text:
[1] Kellan announced the quiz results as though he were reading a storm warning. "Blue team: forty-eight. Gold team: FIFTY." He stretched the last word until even the custodian looked up. Kellan was Gold’s captain.
[2] On the noticeboard he drew Blue’s bar two squares high and Gold’s four squares high. The bars began at forty-six, though the small label was almost under the frame. Priya stared at the picture. "We didn’t score twice as much," she said.
[3] Kellan redrew the display from zero. Now the bars nearly touched in height. He kept the two-point difference in large print above them. Invented display comparison. Scores: Blue 48 points; Gold 50 points. Display A uses a baseline of 46, with one square per point above 46: Blue has 2 squares and Gold 4. Display B begins at 0, with one square per 2 points: Blue has 24 squares and Gold 25. These descriptions fully specify the bars.

passages.title: Three hours on one street — literature
passages.text:
[1] Esme stacked the meeting chairs in twelve minutes. The manager wrote 12 MINUTES beside her name, then asked why the next volunteer needed twenty. Esme looked at the second room. Its chairs were heavier, and half still held bags.
[2] "Mine were already empty," she said. The manager tapped the number. "It is a record." Esme had been proud of it a moment earlier. Now the number seemed to have borrowed her voice and begun ordering other people around.
[3] She added a line beneath the time: light chairs, clear floor, no bags. The other volunteer wrote his conditions too. On the new chart, their numbers no longer stood alone. Esme kept her twelve minutes, but nobody had to race a version of her that existed only on paper.

passages.title: Three hours on one street — information
passages.text:
Original historical display and commentary based only on h. Timeline: 9:00 — Franklin offers a shilling for sweeping the street. 12:00 — the worker returns for payment. After that — a servant reports the street swept clean and dust placed in the middle gutter. Later rain — the account says the dust washes away. The last two events have no exact times in the excerpt.
Commentary: Franklin then judges that a stronger worker might finish in half the time. The observed episode concerns one worker, one street, and one set of conditions. The estimate is not a second timed trial. His description of the worker as feeble is his judgment, not a supplied medical measurement. Read the source as historical testimony and reasoning, not as a modern labor benchmark.

passages.title: Franklin — historical source excerpt
passages.text:
An accidental occurrence had instructed me how much sweeping might be done in a little time. I found at my door in Craven-street, one morning, a poor woman sweeping my pavement with a birch broom; she appeared very pale and feeble, as just come out of a fit of sickness. I ask'd who employ'd her to sweep there; she said, "Nobody, but I am very poor and in distress, and I sweeps before gentle-folkses doors, and hopes they will give me something." I bid her sweep the whole street clean, and I would give her a shilling; this was at nine o'clock; at 12 she came for the shilling. From the slowness I saw at first in her working, I could scarce believe that the work was done so soon, and sent my servant to examine it, who reported that the whole street was swept perfectly clean, and all the dust plac'd in the gutter, which was in the middle; and the next rain wash'd it quite away, so that the pavement and even the kennel were perfectly clean.

I then judg'd that, if that feeble woman could sweep such a street in three hours, a strong, active man might have done it in half the time.

passages.text:
Original historical fiction inspired by source h; the bystander and her thoughts are invented, not a historical witness account.
[1] I was carrying folded cloth past the baker’s when a young stranger emerged with bread tucked under both arms. He took a determined bite from a third roll. I thought he must be showing off how much he could buy. My own parcel looked suddenly small.
[2] At the corner he turned as though the streets had rearranged themselves. I slowed, expecting him to ask a direction, but he continued toward the water. Later I saw him give two rolls to a woman beside a child. The parcel under my arm had not changed weight, but I felt foolish for measuring his life by the size of his breakfast.
[3] I did not learn his name that morning. If I told the story afterward, I would have to admit that the first thing I knew about him was something I had invented.

Original paired interpretations based only on h. [A] The episode emphasizes a newcomer’s unfamiliarity. Franklin asks for bread types or prices the baker cannot supply, misunderstands local money and quantity, and carries rolls awkwardly. His later knowledge makes the remembered scene humorous.
[B] The episode also presents generosity after need is satisfied. Franklin eats one roll and gives the other two to a woman and child from the boat. passages.title: Franklin — historical source excerpt
passages.text: Then I walked up the street, gazing about till near the market-house I met a boy with bread. I had made many a meal on bread, and, inquiring where he got it, I went immediately to the baker's he directed me to, in Second-street, and ask'd for bisket, intending such as we had in Boston; but they, it seems, were not made in Philadelphia. Then I asked for a three-penny loaf, and was told they had none such. So not considering or knowing the difference of money, and the greater cheapness nor the names of his bread, I bade him give me three-penny worth of any sort. He gave me, accordingly, three great puffy rolls. I was surpris'd at the quantity, but took it, and, having no room in my pockets, walk'd off with a roll under each arm, and eating the other. Thus I went up Market-street as far as Fourth-street, passing by the door of Mr. Read, my future wife's father; when she, standing at the door, saw me, and thought I made, as I certainly did, a most awkward, ridiculous appearance. Then I turned and went down Chestnut-street and part of Walnut-street, eating my roll all the way, and, coming round, found myself again at Market-street wharf, near the boat I came in, to which I went for a draught of the river water; and, being filled with one of my rolls, gave the other two to a woman and her child that came down the river in the boat with us, and were waiting to go farther.

passages.text:
Original historical fiction inspired by h; Mara and the dialogue are invented.
[1] Mara spread sentence notes across the printshop table. Yesterday she had copied an essay so neatly that she could almost see the original page with her eyes closed. Today her uncle told her to turn the model face down. The notes seemed to belong to different stories.
[2] She arranged the conclusion first because it sounded grand. When she read aloud, her uncle asked, "What question have you answered?" Mara looked for it and found that she had placed it near the end. She wanted to blame the scraps for moving.
[3] At dusk she unfolded the original. Its sequence was clearer than hers, but her second attempt had one transition she preferred. She circled that sentence and marked three places needing revision. The model no longer looked like a wall she could only trace. It looked like a door whose hinges she might learn to understand.

Original paired method commentaries. [A] Franklin’s account supports deliberate imitation: he admires a model, makes hints, reconstructs passages, and compares his work against the original. Comparison helps him identify faults.
[B] It also supports active transformation: he turns prose into verse and back, shuffles hints, and restores an order. These tasks require choices rather than copying visible sentences. B cautions that "imitation" is incomplete if it means mechanical copying. Neither commentary reports a classroom experiment; both interpret the autobiographical method supplied in h.

passages.title: Franklin — historical source excerpt
passages.text: About this time I met with an odd volume of the Spectator. It was the third. I had never before seen any of them. I bought it, read it over and over, and was much delighted with it. I thought the writing excellent, and wished, if possible, to imitate it. With this view I took some of the papers, and, making short hints of the sentiment in each sentence, laid them by a few days, and then, without looking at the book, try'd to compleat the papers again, by expressing each hinted sentiment at length, and as fully as it had been expressed before, in any suitable words that should come to hand. Then I compared my Spectator with the original, discovered some of my faults, and corrected them. But I found I wanted a stock of words, or a readiness in recollecting and using them, which I thought I should have acquired before that time if I had gone on making verses; since the continual occasion for words of the same import, but of different length, to suit the measure, or of different sound for the rhyme, would have laid me under a constant necessity of searching for variety, and also have tended to fix that variety in my mind, and make me master of it. Therefore I took some of the tales and turned them into verse; and, after a time, when I had pretty well forgotten the prose, turned them back again. I also sometimes jumbled my collections of hints into confusion, and after some weeks endeavored to reduce them into the best order, before I began to form the full sentences and compleat the paper. This was to teach me method in the arrangement of thoughts. By comparing my work afterwards with the original, I discovered many faults and amended them; but I sometimes had the pleasure of fancying that, in certain particulars of small import, I had been lucky enough to improve the method of the language, and this encouraged me to think I might possibly in time come to be a tolerable English writer, of which I was extremely ambitious. My time for these exercises and for reading was at night, after work or before it began in the morning, or on Sundays, when I contrived to be in the printing-house alone, evading as much as I could the common attendance on public worship which my father used to exact of me when I was under his care, and which indeed I still thought a duty, thought I could not, as it seemed to me, afford time to practise it.

passages.text:
Original historical fiction inspired by h. The apprentice and conversation are invented, not documented events.
[1] The apprentice Owen stood outside the lending room on its open day, watching a subscriber tuck a book into a cloth bag. He had imagined shelves meant a place where anyone could choose a volume. His employer explained the entrance payment and yearly contribution. Owen counted the coins he had saved for new shoes.
[2] Inside, two tradesmen debated which book to borrow. Owen could hear them disagreeing about a passage as comfortably as men discussed timber in the yard. He had never heard books spoken of that way. The door seemed more open and more closed than he had expected.
[3] His employer offered to discuss a borrowed chapter after work. Owen accepted, but kept his own coin list. Hearing a chapter was not the same as choosing one. He left with both a new opportunity and a clearer name for what he still lacked.

passages.text:
Original paired historical interpretations of h. [A] The library widened access by pooling subscriptions and importing books for lending. Franklin names mostly young tradesmen among the initial fifty supporters and describes later donations. Shared access could offer more than each member could buy alone.
[B] That expansion had conditions. Members paid forty shillings initially and ten annually; lending occurred one day a week to subscribers, with a return obligation. The source does not show free access for every resident. A and B can both be accurate because expanded access and universal access are different claims.
